questions.question: What is the best first question before ordering a diagnostic test?
choices: Is the test available in the EHR?
What target condition and clinical decision will this test address, and how would each possible result change management?
Can the largest available panel be ordered?
Does the patient expect laboratory testing?
questions.explanation: Testing should begin with a defined diagnostic target and decision; if no plausible result changes care, the test may add burden without utility.

questions.question: Pretest probability is 10%, and a positive result has LR+ 6. Approximately what is the post-test probability?
questions.explanation: Pretest odds are 0.10/0.90 = 0.111; multiplied by 6 gives 0.666 odds, which converts to about 40% probability.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes clinical utility from diagnostic accuracy?
choices: Clinical utility asks whether using the test improves decisions or patient outcomes compared with alternatives
Clinical utility is another name for sensitivity
Accuracy always proves clinical utility
Clinical utility applies only to genetic testing
questions.explanation: Accuracy describes classification performance; utility requires evidence that the testing pathway changes care in a way that produces worthwhile outcomes.

questions.question: A diagnostic study applies the reference standard mainly to patients with positive index tests. What is the major concern?
choices: Recall bias only
The prevalence is automatically zero
The index test becomes a treatment
Partial verification bias may hide false negatives and distort accuracy
questions.explanation: If test-negative patients are not adequately verified, missed disease may remain unknown and sensitivity or specificity estimates can be biased.

questions.question: Why can a positive screening test have low positive predictive value in a very low-prevalence population?
choices: Sensitivity becomes negative
False positives may outnumber true positives when the target condition is rare
Specificity is always zero in screening
Predictive values never depend on prevalence
questions.explanation: Even a relatively specific test can generate more false than true positives when few people in the screened population have the condition.

questions.question: What is overdiagnosis?
choices: Any incorrect positive result
Failure to communicate a result
Detection of a real condition that would not have caused symptoms or harm during the patient's lifetime
An indeterminate laboratory value
questions.explanation: Overdiagnosis is not a false positive; the abnormality is real, but its detection cannot benefit the patient and may trigger unnecessary treatment.

questions.question: What is required before a clinical prediction rule is safely transported into a different population?
choices: External validation showing appropriate performance, calibration, and applicability in the new context
A memorable acronym
A high score in the derivation dataset only
Publication on social media
questions.explanation: Derivation performance is optimistic; external validation assesses whether the rule transports to new patients, settings, measurements, and prevalence.

questions.question: Which statement about reference intervals is correct?
choices: Every value outside the interval proves disease
Every value inside excludes disease
Reference intervals and treatment thresholds are always identical
Some healthy people fall outside a reference interval, so results require clinical and method context
questions.explanation: Reference intervals commonly describe a selected population distribution and are not automatic diagnostic or treatment boundaries.

questions.question: Which best describes diagnostic stewardship?
choices: Ordering fewer tests regardless of risk
Using the right test for the right patient and timing, interpreting it correctly, and ensuring reliable action and follow-up
Avoiding all confirmatory testing
Allowing the laboratory alone to choose the diagnosis
questions.explanation: Stewardship balances under- and over-testing across selection, specimen, analysis, interpretation, communication, action, and follow-up.

questions.question: A patient is clinically unstable but a risk score labels them low risk. What should the FNP do?
choices: Discharge based on the score
Repeat the score until it rises
Recognize the rule is not a substitute for instability assessment and arrange urgent evaluation
Ignore all future prediction rules
questions.explanation: Prediction tools apply only within validated conditions; hemodynamic or clinical instability requires immediate assessment and escalation regardless of a score.
